mcqs.question: Two users start from the same document text. User A inserts text at offset 5; concurrently, User B deletes a range at offsets 6-11. If both ops are applied literally at their original offsets, what goes wrong?
options: Nothing goes wrong — offsets are absolute positions and don't change
The server rejects the second op automatically
Both edits are silently merged into a single character
A's insertion shifts the text, so B's delete now targets the wrong range and corrupts or misfires
mcqs.explanation: Offsets are only valid relative to the document state they were computed against; once A's insert shifts everything after offset 5, B's original offsets 6-11 point at different text. There's no automatic server rejection and no silent single-character merge — this is exactly the corruption OT and CRDTs exist to prevent.

mcqs.question: What is the key structural difference that lets a CRDT merge concurrent edits without a central server deciding op order?
options: The data structure is designed so any order of applying ops produces the same result, using stable position identifiers instead of fragile numeric offsets
CRDTs simply retry failed merges until one succeeds
CRDTs require every client to have identical network latency
CRDTs store the entire document history as plain text diffs
mcqs.explanation: CRDTs achieve order-independence by construction — commutative merge logic built on stable identifiers (e.g. per-character position IDs) rather than positions that shift as the document changes. There's no retry loop, no latency requirement, and CRDTs aren't defined by storing plain-text diffs.

mcqs.question: A client stays offline for 3 days while continuing to edit locally. Why does this make reconciliation on reconnect harder than a 30-second offline gap?
options: Offline duration doesn't affect reconciliation difficulty at all
The client must discard all local edits made during the outage
The buffered local ops must be merged against a much larger volume of ops that happened server-side during the gap, increasing the chance and complexity of conflicts
The document automatically locks after 24 hours offline
mcqs.explanation: Reconciliation cost scales with how much divergence accumulated — more time offline usually means more server-side ops to merge against, and more opportunity for genuinely conflicting edits. Local edits aren't discarded (that would defeat offline support), and there's no automatic 24-hour lock in this design.
